newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures failed to break out of the narrow range they've been stuck in since last week and traders saw a similar trend continuing ahead of remarks by U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan on Wednesday.
The March bond future oscillated within in a nine-tick range, local traders providing most of the activity in the absence of any major market-moving events.

The contract gnawed at the edge of a gap which has capped the market for four sessions but lacked the momentum to make any significant inroads, leaving a hole between 132.38-42 which still needs to be hurdled convincingly, traders said.

The contract settled up 0.12 at 132.24, smack in the middle of the 132.38-42 gap and an area of support between 131.96 and 132.04. Traders said the contract had failed to fill the lower gap on Monday, despite repeated efforts, and had failed similarly today to fill the upper gap.
"Without any unexpected news we should stay in this corrective phase tomorrow," said a trader in Paris.

Greenspan's testimony on the economy and monetary policy to the Senate Banking Committee was due to start at 1500 GMT on Wednesday and will be closely watched by financial markets for any clues as to official thinking on the need for rate rises.

PIBOR contracts also remained in a narrow range. The March contract has been stuck between 96.64 and 96.67 for three sessions and hopes for rate cuts at the Bank of France monetary policy council meeting on Thursday have all but evaporated with the recent rise in the dollar.

June fared somewhat better early on Tuesday, with some traders citing the mild reversal of the dollar's heady rally this week as the reason for the more optimismic outlook. However a late sell-off left June unchanged at 96.66.
The franc was relatively steady against the mark at 3.3739 but off earlier lows of 3.3703 per mark.

Traders said there was little reaction to the rise in the French inflation rate in January to 1.8 percent. The National Statistics Institute INSEE said the increase in the year-on-year rate from 1.7 percent was largely due to a sharp rise in food prices because of the unusually cold weather at the beginning of the year.
The announcement of a French record 122 billion franc trade surplus in 1996, and hopes for a better performance in 1997, left traders equally unmoved.
Call money was unchanged at 3-1/8 1/4 percent.
